The visit witnessed participation from
Shri Puran Kumar Gurung
, Hon’ble Minister for Fisheries, AH&VS and Dairying, Agriculture & Horticulture, Government of Sikkim;
Dr. Abhilaksh Likhi
, Secretary (Fisheries), Department of Fisheries, Government of India, High level officials from Sikkim state government, NFBD, ICAR Institutes, fish farmers, fisheries cooperatives and other relevant fisheries stakeholders.
the Union Minister visited the
Live Fish Vending Centre supported under PMMSY
and interacted with members of the Fish Farmers’ Cooperative Societies to understand the challenges faced on ground. Fish feed was distributed to 15 fish farmers from two fisheries cooperative societies, reinforcing support for fish production and farmer-based institutions. The Minister also inspected stalls showcasing fish, ornamental fish and value-added fish products, along with dairy and animal products and locally grown organic vegetables, highlighting the diversity of livelihood and market opportunities in the region.
During the program, the Union Minister
launched the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for Organic Certification of Fisheries in the Northeastern region
and inaugurated projects worth
₹375 lakh under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY)
, encompassing critical fisheries infrastructure such as hatcheries, feed mills, cold storage facilities and production-related technologies such as Biofloc and Recirculatory Aquaculture system (RAS). The projects inaugurated under PMMSY will strengthen critical links across the fisheries value chain. Kisan Credit Cards were distributed to fish farmers for facilitate access to institutional credit, while cheques were provided to five fish farmers under the Mukhya Mantri Matsya Uthpadhan Yojana (MMMUY), further strengthening financial support for fish farmers and fisheries-based livelihoods.
The Government has adopted a
cluster-based approach for integrated development of the fisheries value chain
, bringing together production, processing, value addition and marketing within identified geographical areas. Under PMMSY, 34 fisheries production and processing clusters have been notified across the country, including organic fisheries clusters in Sikkim and Meghalaya.
Soreng District, Sikkim is
India’s first Organic Fisheries Cluster
launched under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY). The cluster focuses on ecologically healthy fish farming without the use of harmful chemicals, antibiotics and pesticides, with special emphasis on Amur carp, Indian Major Carps (IMC) and Trout. It seeks to build on Sikkim’s established organic ecosystem while strengthening the fisheries value chain, enhancing incomes of fish farmers and creating opportunities for premium domestic and international markets for organic fish and fish products.
The SOP for Organic Certification of Fisheries in the Northeastern region will further strengthen this ecosystem by providing a structured framework for organic production and supporting traceability across the value chain. By developing a more credible and market-oriented organic fisheries ecosystem, the initiative will enhance the positioning of organic fish products and support their access to premium domestic and export markets.
Sikkim has taken a pioneering step towards strengthening market linkages by entering an MoU with Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) for institutional procurement of locally produced Rainbow Trout. The initiative seeks to provide a stable market for trout farmers while strengthening the value chain for this high value Coldwater fish. The proposed arrangement envisages regular supply of trout to ITBP establishments, with emphasis on quality specifications, supply capacity, pricing, inspection and supply schedules.
The visit to Sikkim underscored the Government’s focus on outcome-oriented development of fisheries in the Northeastern Region, with convergence of Central and State initiatives and active engagement of fish farmers and institutions. The interventions are expected to translate the region’s fisheries potential into higher farmer incomes, stronger local enterprise and sustainable economic opportunities, while contributing to the larger objective of inclusive growth in the region.

The visit of the Hon’ble Union Minister underscores the Government of India's recognition of Sikkim's contribution and its importance in the dairy and animal husbandry sectors. The infrastructure and initiatives being undertaken are expected to strengthen the livelihoods of farmers and livestock rearers, promote value addition, improve supply-chain infrastructure and create new opportunities for income generation. title: Union Health Minister Shri J.P. Nadda inaugurates Advanced Radiotherapy Facility at AIIMS Rajkot, reaffirms commitment to quality cancer care for every citizen
subtitle:
Investment of approximately ₹39 crore in advanced cancer care infrastructure at AIIMS Rajkot strengthens tertiary healthcare under Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana

Shri Nadda highlights expansion of AIIMS and nationwide cancer screening, with 37.7 crore oral cancer screenings conducted

Shri Praful Pansheriya, MoS Health, Government of Gujarat, welcomes advanced radiotherapy services in Rajkot, expresses gratitude to Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi for strengthening regional healthcare

Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava highlights comprehensive healthcare under National Health Policy 2017, more than 1.8 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs and measures to make cancer medicines affordable

Advanced Radiotherapy Facility to serve an estimated 1.54 crore people, with an anticipated annual patient load of 500–700 cases
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                02 NOV 2026 6:17PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare, Shri Jagat Prakash Nadda, today inaugurated and dedicated to the nation the Advanced Radiotherapy Facility at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Rajkot. Equipped with advanced radiation therapy technologies, the facility marks an important step towards improving access to specialised cancer care for people across Rajkot and the wider Saurashtra region.
With an investment of approximately ₹39 crore, the facility at AIIMS Rajkot has been established under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY). The endeavour reflects the Union Government’s continued efforts to address regional imbalances in the availability of tertiary healthcare services.
Addressing the gathering, Shri J.P. Nadda said that cancer imposes a significant medical, emotional, social and financial burden on patients and their families. He emphasised that timely treatment is critical and that no person should be deprived of quality cancer care because of their location or financial circumstances. The Minister noted that the new facility would particularly benefit people from Saurashtra and Kutch, who previously had to travel to distant cities such as Ahmedabad and Mumbai for specialised treatment. He described the facility as a major step towards improving access to cancer care in the region.
Shri Nadda highlighted the expansion of AIIMS under Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, noting that India has progressed from one AIIMS in New Delhi to 18 operational institutions out of 22, significantly strengthening access to specialised tertiary healthcare. He also emphasised the need for seamless linkages across levels of healthcare to ensure patients receive appropriate treatment.
Emphasising prevention and early detection, Shri Nadda highlighted screening initiatives undertaken through Ayushman Arogya Mandirs. Since 2018, approximately 44 crore screenings each have been conducted for hypertension and diabetes, while around 37.7 crore people have been screened for oral cancer, with approximately 2.5 lakh cases detected. Breast cancer screening has covered around 17.7 crore women, identifying approximately 95,000 cases, while 9.8 crore women have been screened for cervical cancer, with around one lakh cases detected. He noted that early detection enables patients to access treatment sooner and improves the prospects of recovery.
The Minister also referred to findings cited from a Lancet report indicating that 90 per cent of cancer patients begin treatment within 30 days. He attributed the improvement in timely access to treatment in part to the expansion of financial protection through Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY), which has enabled economically vulnerable patients to seek treatment without the same financial constraints. Eligible AB PM-JAY beneficiaries at AIIMS Rajkot will be able to access cancer treatment at no cost, while other patients will receive treatment at subsidised rates to minimise financial burden.
Shri Praful Pansheriya, Minister of State for Health, Family Welfare and Medical Education, Government of Gujarat (Independent Charge), welcomed the inauguration and expressed gratitude to Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi for strengthening healthcare facilities in the region. He said that the advanced radiotherapy facility would be of considerable benefit to people across Saurashtra.
Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava, Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, described the inauguration as an important milestone in AIIMS Rajkot's development and a significant step towards the vision of Viksit Bharat articulated by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. She highlighted the National Health Policy 2017, formulated under the guidance of the Union Health Minister, which envisages comprehensive healthcare encompassing preventive, promotive, curative, rehabilitative and palliative services, with Universal Health Coverage as a national goal.
Smt. Srivastava noted that the Government has strengthened healthcare infrastructure through more than 1.8 lakh Ayushman Arogya Mandirs and the Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission. She highlighted AIIMS Rajkot's contribution to advanced treatment and research, cancer screening initiatives under the Swasth Nari Sashakt Parivar campaign and measures to improve the affordability of cancer medicines, including trade margin rationalisation, AMRIT pharmacies, Jan Aushadhi Kendras and basic customs duty exemptions. She also noted the availability of CAR-T cell therapy at affordable rates in India.
Dr. J.S. Titiyal, President, AIIMS Rajkot, described the facility as an important addition to cancer care in the region and commended the Government of India and Gujarat Government for their support, along with the faculty, doctors, nurses and technical staff for establishing the service.
The Advanced Radiotherapy Facility is expected to serve a catchment population of approximately 1.54 crore people across Saurashtra, including Rajkot, Jamnagar, Junagadh, Porbandar, Amreli, Bhavnagar, Morbi, Surendranagar, Gir Somnath, Devbhumi Dwarka and Botad. This benefits the region which largely comprises rural, semi-urban and economically weaker communities.
The facility is equipped with a High Energy Linear Accelerator (LINAC), a Wide Bore CT Simulator and a High Dose Rate (HDR) Brachytherapy Unit. The LINAC enables advanced techniques such as Intensity Modulated Radiotherapy (IMRT), Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT), Image Guided Radiotherapy (IGRT), Stereotactic Radiosurgery (SRS), Stereotactic Radiotherapy (SRT) and Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy (SBRT), supporting precise delivery of radiation with millimetre-level accuracy. The Wide Bore CT Simulator supports three-dimensional treatment planning imaging, while HDR brachytherapy enables targeted internal radiation treatment for gynaecological cancers, head and neck cancers, sarcomas and other tumours.
The Department of Radiation Oncology functions within an integrated cancer care framework, supported by chemotherapy and surgical services, including head and neck, orthopaedic, gynaecological oncology and general surgery. This multidisciplinary arrangement allows patients to receive different forms of cancer treatment within a single institution.
Operational since 29 May 2026, the department has begun providing radiotherapy and chemotherapy services. The facility is expected to initially manage approximately 500–700 cases annually, with a focus on head and neck, gynaecological, breast, bone and soft tissue and other malignancies.
The programme was also attended by Shri Parshottambhai Rupala and Shri Kesridevsinh Jhala, Members of Parliament; Dr. L.N. Dorairajan, Executive Director, AIIMS Rajkot; and other senior officials from the Ministry of Health, faculty members and healthcare professionals.

Identifying this need, Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation, Shri Amit Shah has directed to establish FRROs in all state capitals by 2027.
Pursuant to the above directions of the Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah, five new FRROs have been set-up in the capitals of five states since 2025. Three FRRO offices at Jaipur, Chandigarh and Guwahati were established in the year 2025. Earlier, these were under the jurisdiction of the FRRO offices located at Delhi, Amritsar and Kolkata respectively.
This year two new FRRO offices have been established in the state capitals, namely, Aizawl (Mizoram), and Amravati (Andhra Pradesh). Earlier, Aizawl was under the jurisdiction of FRRO, Kolkata whereas Amravati was under the jurisdiction of FRRO, Hyderabad. Recently three new FRRO offices namely Kohima (Nagaland), Agartala (Tripura) and Bhubaneshwar (Odisha) are notified. Earlier, Kohima and Agartala were under the jurisdiction of FRRO, Kolkata whereas Bhubaneshwar was under the jurisdiction of FRRO, Hyderabad.
The total number of FRRO offices in the country has now gone up to twenty (20), located at Ahmedabad, Amravati, Amritsar, Aizawl, Agartala, Bengaluru, Bhubaneswar, Calicut, Chennai, Cochin, Chandigarh, Delhi, Guwahati, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Kohima, Kozhikode, Lucknow, Mumbai and Trivandrum.
The Government of India is pursuing the matter of establishing FRRO’s in remaining States namely Bihar, Goa, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya. This will help foreigners visiting India in obtaining various consular services such as visa extension, conversion, immigration compliance and legal safety. The expansion will strengthen local-level institutional capacity, improve coordination with State authorities, facilitate legitimate foreign visitors and reinforce the effective implementation of immigration law and national security requirements.
The expansion of Foreigners Regional Registration Offices (FRROs) has a dual focus on facilitating foreigners’ legitimate travel and stay in India and ensuring effective implementation of immigration laws and security requirements. The Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, which consolidated four earlier laws relating to immigration and foreigners, provides a unified statutory framework for regulating the entry, stay, movement and exit of foreign nationals. As per this act, the Bureau of Immigration, which mainly performs the immigration function, shall in discharge of its duties, be assisted, among others, by the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer (FRRO) as may be authorized by the Central Government of India.
The Foreigners Regional Registration Office regulates, tracks and facilitates the lawful stay of foreign nationals visiting or residing in India. It administers post-arrival registration for eligible category of foreigners and issues a Registration Certificate (RC)/Residential Permit on registration. It also records changes in a foreigner’s particulars, such as residential address, passport details or travel plans within the country, and grants permission to visit protected and restricted areas. Exit permits are issued to foreigners whose visas have expired, who have overstayed, or who require formal clearance before leaving India. Overall, the FRRO monitors compliance with Indian immigration laws, handles cases of overstay and visa violations, and coordinates legal action or penalties where necessary.

title: Lending Institutions propose institutional financing of PMAY-G beneficiaries at MoRD–NHB “PMAY-G Reform Samvad” in Lonavala: States, HFCs, SFBs, MFIs and RRBs deliberate a roadmap for affordable institutional credit for rural housing
date:
Posted On:
                02 NOV 2026 9:22PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD), jointly with the National Housing Bank (NHB), spearheaded “PMAY-G Reform Samvad”, a one-day stakeholder dialogue on reforms for strengthening rural housing under PMAY-G. It brought together MoRD, NHB, State Rural Development Departments, the World Bank, International Finance Corporation, Sa-Dhan, TCIS Habitat for Humanity International and lending institutions, including Housing Finance Companies (HFCs), Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), Small Finance Banks (SFBs) and Micro Finance Institutions (MFIs).
Departing from the conventional view for rural loans, the discussion witnessed the lenders describing PMAY-G households as a promising and largely untapped segment. They noted that beneficiaries are verified under the scheme, Government assistance covers a substantial part of the cost, and construction is tracked through milestones on the PMAY-G platform, which reduces the cost and risk of lending. They expressed willingness to design dedicated loan products and to work with the Ministry, NHB and States on enabling reforms.
Earlier in the morning, Dr. Rajaram Dighe, Director, Rural Housing, Government of Maharashtra, welcomed the participants. Shri Sanjay Shukla, Managing Director, NHB, underlined the need for affordable institutional credit to help rural families complete their homes. Shri Piyush Srivastava, Senior Economic Advisor (Rural Housing), MoRD, delivered the keynote address, setting the direction for the day. He mentioned that PMAY-G was the world’s largest housing scheme and its achievements in rural housing are a matter of great satisfaction.  He, however, called for greater coordinated push towards the national goal of housing for all where the institutional finance can act as a force multiplier. NHB, the World Bank, Sa-Dhan and TCIS Habitat for Humanity International then presented global and grassroots perspectives on rural housing finance.
Why institutional credit matters for PMAY-G
PMAY-G aims to complete 4.95 crore pucca houses by March 2029. The cost of building a rural house often exceeds the assistance under the scheme, and arranging the balance can delay construction and push households towards high-interest informal lenders. Lenders with last-mile reach, in turn, face funding gaps, perceived credit risk and the absence of standardised rural housing loan products. The Samvad deliberated on:
which household segments can be financed responsibly, with loan sizes and repayment suited to seasonal incomes;
the barriers to lending, from documentation and appraisal to transaction costs;
how PMAY-G data, construction milestones and DAY-NRLM SHG networks can lower these barriers; and
the support needed from the Centre, States and NHB, including NHB’s proposed refinance window for rural housing.
Three mixed breakout groups of lenders and State Governments presented their recommendations in plenary, followed by an open forum.
Key Outcomes of the Deliberations
A key takeaway was the keen interest of HFCs, SFBs and MFIs in extending credit to PMAY-G beneficiaries over and above scheme assistance. Lenders cited unclear land titles, restrictions on mortgage of allotted properties, seasonal incomes, high transaction costs and perceived credit risk as the main barriers. To translate this interest into lending at scale, participants recommended:
Dedicated rural housing loan products
of ₹2–5 lakh, with repayment aligned to seasonal incomes;
A pilot
of a commercially viable model, possibly anchored by an NHB-supported entity, before wider rollout;
Credit guarantee support
through a Government-backed partial guarantee mechanism;
Affordable lending rates
through interest subvention, concessional funding and NHB refinance;
Land and property reforms
by States, including mortgage of allotted properties and stamp duty concessions;
Regulatory treatment suited to rural borrowers
, including differentiated NPA and provisioning norms; and
Community-based last-mile delivery
through Gram Panchayats, DAY-NRLM SHGs and the LokOS platform.
Review of PMAY-G progress
The workshop also reviewed PMAY-G progress in Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Assam and Kerala, including a dedicated session with PFMS to resolve State-specific SNA SPARSH issues.
Way forward
The interest shown by lending institutions marks an important step towards combining Government assistance with institutional credit, so that PMAY-G families can complete quality homes without costly informal borrowing. The Ministry will examine the suggestions emerging from the Samvad and take them forward in consultation with NHB, State Governments, lending institutions and knowledge partners.

title: Ministry of Rural Development Notifies Grievance Redressal Rules, 2026 under VB–G RAM G Act
subtitle:
Multi-tier mechanism and digital platform for prompt, transparent, and time-bound grievance redressal

Multiple channels for grievance submission, mandatory registration, digital tracking and escalation of unresolved grievances

Enquiry to be completed within 7 working days and grievances to be resolved within 15 days
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                02 NOV 2026 11:16AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India, has notified the Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin): VB–G RAM G – Grievance Redressal Rules, 2026, establishing a structured, multi-tier and time-bound mechanism for addressing grievances relating to the implementation of the Scheme. The Rules aim to make grievance redressal more accessible, transparent and accountable, while ensuring that citizens' concerns receive timely attention and appropriate action.
Multi-tier grievance redressal mechanism
The Rules provide for the establishment of a time-bound, multi-tier grievance redressal mechanism by State Governments at the Gram Panchayat, Block and District levels. Designated Grievance Redressal Officers at the appropriate levels will be responsible for receiving, registering, enquiring into and disposing of grievances.
The District Programme Coordinator will oversee grievance redressal at the district level and ensure that grievances are addressed through the designated mechanism and the Digital Public Infrastructure for grievance redressal.
Multiple channels for submission of grievances
To facilitate easy access, any person may submit a grievance relating to any matter arising out of or connected with the implementation of the Scheme. The Rules provide for submission of grievances through multiple channels:
In person before the designated Grievance Redressal Officer;
Through speed post, with proof of delivery;
Through the Digital Public Infrastructure for Redressal of Grievances designated by the Central Government; and
Through telephone, designated helplines or any other mode decided by the State Government.
Grievances received in physical form at the Gram Panchayat, Block or District level must be entered and registered on the designated Digital Public Infrastructure on the day of receipt or, where this is not feasible, by the next working day.
Upon registration, the complainant will receive an acknowledgement containing the registration number, date of receipt and designation of the receiving authority. The acknowledgement will be provided electronically in cases of digital submission and in physical form where the grievance is received physically.
Importantly, no grievance can be refused registration on the grounds of its format, language, manner of submission or any procedural deficiency. This provision ensures that citizens can access the grievance redressal mechanism without being hindered by procedural requirements.
Defined timelines for enquiry and resolution
The Rules prescribe clear timelines to ensure prompt examination and resolution of grievances. The designated Grievance Redressal Officer is required to examine every registered grievance and undertake the necessary enquiry. For this purpose, the officer may call for relevant records, registers, documents, reports, electronic data or other information from the concerned authorities or functionaries.
Where necessary, the complainant will be provided a reasonable opportunity to be heard, either in person or through electronic means, before the grievance is disposed of.
The enquiry into a grievance is required to be completed within seven working days from the date of its receipt. Upon completion of the enquiry, the Grievance Redressal Officer will record the findings and take, or cause to be taken, appropriate corrective or remedial action in accordance with the Act and the Rules. The grievance is required to be resolved within 15 days from the date of its receipt.
The findings and action taken will be recorded on the designated Digital Public Infrastructure and communicated to the complainant. Where a grievance has been received in physical form, its outcome and the action taken will also be communicated to the complainant in physical form.
Digital tracking and escalation of unresolved grievances
The designated Digital Public Infrastructure will facilitate end-to-end tracking of grievances, from registration to final disposal. It will also enable electronic recording of the enquiry, findings and action taken, thereby strengthening transparency and accountability in the grievance redressal process.
Any grievance that remains unresolved within the prescribed period of 15 days will be escalated to the next higher level through the grievance redressal mechanism established by the State Government. The authority receiving the escalated grievance will examine the matter and take appropriate action for its disposal. Such grievances will continue to be monitored electronically until their resolution.
Provision for appeals
The Rules also provide for appeals against orders passed under the grievance redressal mechanism. Such appeals will be filed and disposed of in accordance with Schedule I to the VB–G RAM G Act, 2025.
Through these Rules, the Government seeks to institutionalise a citizen-centric, accessible and time-bound grievance redressal framework under VB–G RAM G. The multi-tier institutional mechanism, multiple channels for grievance submission, mandatory registration, defined timelines, digital tracking and escalation of unresolved grievances are expected to strengthen administrative accountability and improve the responsiveness of the Scheme's implementation.
The notification marks an important step towards ensuring that grievances relating to the implementation of VB–G RAM G are addressed systematically, transparently and within prescribed timelines, thereby reinforcing the rights and entitlements of rural households under the Scheme.

title: 24 Years X-ray observations trace the mystery behind one of the brightest X-ray emitters in nearby galaxies
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                02 NOV 2026 4:37PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Astronomers have divulged the mystery behind the changing X-ray behaviour of NGC 4490 ULX-8, one of the brightest X-Ray emitters located in a nearby galaxy, by tracking X-Ray observations over a 24-year period. This can help in understanding the compact objects that power the ULXs and also track the growth of these objects in such extreme environments.
Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are among the brightest X-ray emitters in nearby galaxies, apart from the emission from supermassive black holes in their centres. ULXs are thought to host either neutron stars or black holes that draw in matter from a companion star. As this material falls inward, it heats up and emits intense X-rays. ULXs appear to shine more brightly than expected from the maximum luminosity predicted by a simple balance between gravity pulling matter inward and radiation pushing it outward. This limit, known as the Eddington limit, is often used as a benchmark for how bright an accreting object can be.
Determining the nature of the compact object powering a ULX is crucial for understanding the physics of super-Eddington accretion, powerful outflows of gas, and the growth of compact objects in such extreme environments.
A research team from Indian Institute of Astrophysics ((IIA), the Raman Research Institute, both autonomous institutes of the Department of Science and Technology (DST) along with other institutions discovered long-term spectral changes that point to evolving accretion conditions around the compact object.
The results provide strong evidence that ULX-8 is powered by a black hole accreting matter at rates exceeding the classical Eddington limit. The work demonstrates the value of long-term multi-mission monitoring in uncovering the nature of some of the Universe's brightest X-ray sources.
Fig
: False-colour X-ray images of NGC 4490/85. Left: Image created from Chandra observations. Right: Image created from EPIC-pn and MOS1/2 observations with XMM-Newton.
“We analysed archival and recent observations of ULX-8 in the interacting galaxy pair NGC 4490/4485, obtained with
Chandra
,
XMM-Newton
, and
Swift
space-based X-ray telescopes between 2000 and 2024, enabling one of the longest X-ray studies of this source to date”, explained Aru Beri, a faculty member at IIA and a co-author of the study.
The study revealed that ULX-8 remained an exceptionally luminous X-ray source throughout the 24-year observing period, while its brightness varied substantially over time. Despite these changes, the source showed no evidence for the dramatic transitions between different accretion states that are commonly observed in many black hole X-ray binaries.
Instead, the X-ray emission retained characteristics consistent with a persistently active ultraluminous accretion flow. The results suggest that ULX-8 is most likely powered by a stellar-mass black hole accreting matter at or near the Eddington limit, providing an important laboratory for studying how compact objects can sustain extreme rates of mass accretion and generate enormous amounts of energy.
Future observatories such as European Space Agency's (ESA)
NewAthena
mission and India's proposed next-generation timing and spectroscopy mission
XSat
will provide improved sensitivity and monitoring capabilities for studying ULXs. Continued long-term observations will help reveal how these extreme systems evolve and offer deeper insights into the
physics of super-Eddington accretion
and the nature of some of the brightest X-ray sources in the nearby Universe.
The study which was authored by Tarang Vashisht (a student at IISER Mohali), Aru Beri (Indian Institute of Astrophysics), and researchers from IUCAA and Raman Research Institute, was published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Journal.

content:
The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) today formally recognised 19 reputed institutions as Centres of Excellence-Skills (CoE-Skills). The Certificates of Recognition were presented by Smt. Debashree Mukherjee, Secretary, MSDE, during a ceremony held at Kaushal Bhawan, New Delhi. The recognition is valid from 9 October 2026 to 8 October 2029.
The institutions have been empanelled through the Green Channel provided under the Guidelines for Empanelment of Centres of Excellence-Skills and Vocational Training Centres. The mechanism offers an expedited route for eligible institutions of established standing, including Institutes of National Importance, ITIs upgraded under PM-SETU, and Skilling Centres of Excellence operated or empanelled by Central Ministries, Departments and State Governments. Under this route, institutions submit essential information and their applications are placed directly before the Executive Committee for consideration, without nomination or the regular evaluation process. The mechanism seeks to accelerate empanelment of reputed and high-quality institutions through a streamlined approval process.
The Guidelines were unveiled on 15 July 2026 by Shri Jayant Chaudhary, Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship and Minister of State for Education, Government of India, during the World Youth Skills Day celebrations at Kaushal Bhawan, New Delhi. The Guidelines seek to strengthen the skilling ecosystem through permanent, advanced and industry-aligned training institutions supported by modern infrastructure, technology and strong industry partnerships.
Speaking on the occasion, Smt. Debashree Mukherjee, Secretary, MSDE, said: “The empanelment of these 19 institutions as Centres of Excellence-Skills marks an important step towards building a trusted national network of permanent, advanced and industry-responsive skilling institutions. We are building a repository of the country’s most reputed institutions, distinguished by their domain expertise and delivery excellence, to strengthen skill development outcomes while making skilling aspirational for our youth. These Centres can play a pivotal role in delivering high-quality training, supporting trainers and assessors, strengthening industry linkages and improving outcomes for learners. We look forward to working closely with these institutions to make advanced and future-ready skilling accessible across sectors and regions.”
A CoE-Skills is envisaged as a permanent, advanced and sector-focused training centre capable of delivering high-quality, industry-aligned and outcome-oriented skill training. CoE-Skills may undertake functions spanning advanced and technology-enabled training, assessment, mentorship and career coaching, Training of Trainers and Assessors, industry engagement, and achievement and tracking of post-training outcomes. Their scheme-agnostic empanelment is intended to establish a long-term association and enable optimum utilisation of existing infrastructure, equipment, trainers, assessors and institutional capacity.
The recognition provides formal acknowledgement by MSDE of these institutions’ capabilities within the national skilling ecosystem. Empanelled Centres may be leveraged for skill development initiatives of MSDE, other Central Ministries, State Governments, industry, CSR initiatives and other stakeholders, subject to applicable programme guidelines.
By bringing high-quality institutions and specialised centres into a common national framework, the CoE-Skills initiative will help strengthen advanced training capacity, facilitate wider sharing of institutional expertise and promote credible, industry-responsive and outcome-oriented skilling across the country.

title: National Conference on “Gender Data and Statistics: From Evidence to Policy Insights | MoSPI and UN Women
date:

content:
A one-day National Conference on
“Gender Data and Statistics: From Evidence to Policy Insights”
was organised by Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) in collaboration with UN Women on 2nd November, 2026 in New Delhi. The conference brought together policymakers, representatives from Central Ministries/Departments and State Governments, statisticians, researchers, academic institutions, technical experts and representatives of UN agencies to deliberate on strengthening the analysis and use of gender statistics for evidence-based policymaking.
The conference was organised to deliberate on and disseminate the findings of
Women and Men in India 2025
, a flagship publication of MoSPI, with the aim of deepening the understanding of key findings and their interlinkages across sectors, facilitating discussions among ministries and other stakeholders, and identifying opportunities to strengthen the analytical and policy use of gender statistics.
The conference commenced with a welcome address by
Ms. Shoko Ishikawa
, Country Representative, UN Women India, who emphasised the importance of gender-disaggregated data and bridging the gap between data producers and users.
Mr. Jean-Eric Paque
, Ambassador of the European Union (EU) to India, highlighted the EU–India Strategic Partnership in advancing gender equality and women’s economic participation.
Dr. Preetam B. Yashvant
, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development, also addressed the gathering, followed by
Dr. Dalip Singh, Director General (Central Statistics), MoSPI
, who emphasised identifying gender gaps to inform evidence-based policies.
Dr. Shamika Ravi
, Member, Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister, highlighted progress in welfare delivery and women’s financial empowerment, while stressing the need for improved employment quality, state-level analysis and stronger gender statistics to guide policy reforms. The inaugural session concluded with a vote of thanks by
Ms. Supriya Roy, Additional Director General, MoSPI
, who acknowledged the contributions of speakers, participants and UN Women.
The conference featured
four thematic technical sessions
, focusing on health and survival across the life course; girls’ education, learning and transition; women’s work, wages, formality and care; and women’s livelihoods, enterprises, skills and financial inclusion. The sessions brought together experts, policymakers and practitioners to examine key findings from
Women and Men in India 2025
, identify differences in outcomes between women and men, and explore opportunities for translating statistical evidence into actionable policy insights.
Discussions on health and survival recognised progress in maternal healthcare and essential health services, while highlighting nutritional and adolescent health challenges. The session on girls’ education, learning and transition noted improvements in enrolment, while emphasising gaps in learning outcomes, STEM participation and employment pathways.
Deliberations on women’s work, wages, formality and care acknowledged rising female labour-force participation, while highlighting challenges in job quality, wage disparities and unpaid care work. The session on women’s livelihoods, enterprises, skills and financial inclusion recognised progress in entrepreneurship and financial inclusion, while stressing the need for better access to credit, markets and sustainable livelihoods, alongside women’s agency and safety.
During the valedictory session, Ms. Suhela Khan, Country Programme Manager, Women’s Economic Empowerment, UN Women India, and Ms. Geeta Singh Rathore, Director General (NSS), MoSPI, highlighted the need to address persistent gender disparities in health, education and economic participation, with particular emphasis on quality of employment, unpaid care work and financial inclusion. The discussions also provided valuable inputs for future editions of
Women and Men in India
, particularly the 2026 edition, underscoring the importance of improved measurement of gender gaps, strengthened inter-ministerial coordination and evidence-based policymaking. The conference concluded with a vote of thanks delivered by Ms. Sunitha Bhaskar, Additional Director General, MoSPI.
The conference concluded by reaffirming the importance of strengthening India's gender statistical ecosystem and fostering continued collaboration among government institutions, statistical agencies, researchers and development partners. It underscored the need to translate gender-disaggregated data into meaningful policy insights to support inclusive development and advancing gender equality.

Ministry of Tribal Affairs in collaboration with the ICMR–National Institute of Health Research (ICMR-NIHR), Bhubaneswar under the Janjatiya Health Institutional Transformation (JanHIT) initiative, has organised the 1st of its kind
National Orientation Programme for Tribal Healers on Public Health
on 1–2nd November 2026 at Kanha Shanti Vanam, Hyderabad. The programme was inaugurated at the auditorium of Kanha Shanti Vanam, Hyderabad by Shri. Manish Thakur, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs and Dr. Sanghamitra Pati, Director, ICMR-NIHR, Bhubaneswar in presence of Shri B. M. Santosh, IAS, Special Secretary and Director, Tribal Welfare, Telangana, Dr. V. Samujwala, Director, Tribal Cultural Research & Training Institute (TCR&TI), Telangana, and other senior officials from Ministry of Tribal Affairs and ICMR-NIHR, Bhubaneswar. The launch of this landmark initiative on the first day of the Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas Pakhwada underscores the shared commitment to honouring and empowering India's tribal communities through inclusive health and capacity-building interventions.
The 1st phase of the orientation programme is being attended by around 550 tribal healers nominated by the State Tribal Welfare departments from nine states and UTs of India (Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Karnataka, Keralam, Maharashtra, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli). The orientation programme aims to orient tribal healers on key public health issues and strengthen their understanding of common diseases, early identification of danger signs, and appropriate referral for timely medical care. Recognising the important role of healers in tribal communities, the initiative seeks to enhance their awareness of essential health practices and encourage linkages with the formal healthcare system.
The two-day orientation programme will cover three training modules addressing a wide range of public health concerns. These include communicable and vector-borne diseases, skin diseases, non-communicable diseases, metabolic and blood disorders, liver diseases, and mental health conditions. The sessions will also focus on appropriate referral for snakebites, scorpion & other stings, animal bites, injuries, eye and ear disorders; oral health; and newborn and infant care. The training will also include integrated practice, review sessions, a post-training assessment, and participant feedback to reinforce learning and assess the orientation's effectiveness.
Participants from different states will attend the 2 day programme, with state-wise arrangements for training sessions in regional languages to facilitate effective communication and learning. Experts from AIIMS, ICMR, Quality Control of India, MS Swaminathan Foundation, Amrita Institute, Kochi, IIHMR, Bengaluru and Piramal Swasthya, Maharashtra will be delivering sessions in respective languages for the healers.
By orienting tribal healers on essential health concerns and appropriate referral practices, the programme seeks to promote informed community-level health support and strengthen collaboration between tribal community practices and the formal healthcare system. This structured capacity-building module developed by ICMR-NIHR, Bhubaneswar, with support from MoTA represents a milestone effort to integrate tribal healthcare practices with formal medical systems, particularly as we commemorate Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas.
The programme will conclude on 2nd November 2026 with a closing ceremony and distribution of certificates to participants.

title: Biosphere Reserves in India
subtitle: Celebrating the International Day for Biosphere Reserves
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                02 NOV 2026 6:50PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The International Day for Biosphere Reserves celebrates the vital role these landscapes play in protecting biodiversity while sustaining human livelihoods. India’s 18 notified Biosphere Reserves, including 13 recognised by UNESCO, represent a wide variety of ecosystems, from the Western Ghats to high-altitude deserts and marine habitats. Their conservation efforts are supported by scientific research, community participation and government initiatives, demonstrating how environmental protection and human well-being can coexist.
Balancing Biodiversity Conservation with Sustainable Development
Biodiversity
refers to the variability of living organisms across terrestrial, marine and other aquatic ecosystems. The
Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
recognises three levels of this diversity.
Genetic diversity
refers to variations within a species, such as different rice varieties.
Species diversity
reflects the range of species, such as tigers, elephants and orchids in a forest.
Ecosystem diversity
encompasses different natural habitats, including forests, grasslands, wetlands and coral reefs. Collectively, these levels sustain ecological processes and support life on Earth.
Biosphere reserves
are
areas identified by national governments for conserving biodiversity and promoting sustainable development.
They protect natural habitats, maintain ecological balance and promote the sustainable use of biological resources. Their conservation contributes to food security, water availability, climate resilience and community livelihoods. They also safeguard natural resources for the benefit of future generations.
Recognising their global importance, the
International Day for Biosphere Reserves is observed annually on 3rd November
. Proclaimed by UNESCO, the day highlights the contribution of these reserves to biodiversity conservation and sustainable development. It also promotes awareness of their role in reconciling environmental protection with human well-being.
For India, this observance reflects its commitment to protecting its rich natural heritage. As one of the world's
17 mega-biodiverse countries
, India accounts for approximately
7–8% of recorded species worldwide
, while it occupies only
2.4% of Earth's land area
. Through its network of biosphere reserves, India seeks to strengthen ecological resilience and promote sustainable livelihoods. These efforts reflect the country's commitment to balancing conservation priorities with the developmental needs of local communities.
Biosphere Reserves: Understanding the Concept
Conserving biodiversity requires an approach that considers both natural ecosystems and the communities dependent on them. It also requires scientific research, responsible resource management and cooperation among different stakeholders. Biosphere reserves provide an internationally recognised framework for bringing these objectives together.
Launched in 1971, UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme promotes scientific approaches to improving relationships between people and their environment. Biosphere reserves function as living laboratories for testing and demonstrating sustainable development practices. They also help local communities sustain their livelihoods while living in harmony with nature.
How are Biosphere Reserves Different from Other Protected Areas?
Protected areas
such as National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries primarily focus on protecting wildlife and their habitats under India’s wildlife protection laws.
Biosphere reserves
adopt a broader approach. They connect protected ecosystems with surrounding communities, making biosphere reserves a model for demonstrating how biodiversity and human well-being can coexist.
Functions of Biosphere Reserves
Biosphere reserves pursue 3 main functions:
Conservation:
Protect biodiversity, genetic resources, ecosystems and landscapes, including associated cultural diversity.
Sustainable Economic Development:
Encourage economic and social activities that respect ecological limits and local cultural values.
Scientific Support:
Underpin scientific research, environmental monitoring, education, training and knowledge exchange to improve conservation practices.
The Three Interconnected Zones
Biosphere reserves follow a zonation model that balances different levels of protection and human activity. Each zone serves a distinct purpose, while contributing to the reserve’s overall objectives.
Core Area:
The core area provides the highest level of protection for ecosystems and biodiversity. It conserves habitats, species and genetic diversity while maintaining essential ecological processes. Human activities are strictly limited, with compatible research and monitoring supporting long-term conservation.
Buffer Zone:
The buffer zone surrounds or adjoins the core zone. It accommodates activities compatible with conservation, including environmental education, scientific research and regulated ecotourism. These activities improve ecological understanding while helping reduce pressures on strictly protected areas.
Transition Area:
The transition area supports settlements, livelihoods and sustainable economic activities. Communities can practise responsible agriculture, sustainable forestry, ecotourism and other locally appropriate activities. This area promotes livelihoods while encouraging the sustainable use of natural resources.
Globally, biosphere reserves comprise an average of 18% core zones, 30% buffer zones and 52% transition zones. This distribution reflects their integrated approach to conservation, balancing strict protection with sustainable development.
Did You Know?
UNESCO’s Network of Biosphere Reserves
comprises 797 biosphere reserves across 145 countries. These sites directly benefit around 300 million people who live within these areas. Their ecological significance extends far beyond their geographical footprint. Biosphere reserves cover approximately 5% of Earth’s terrestrial surface, yet sustain over 60% of the world’s terrestrial vertebrate species richness. As per
the Map of the World Network of Biosphere Reserves 2025-26
, about 40% of Biosphere reserves may face more extreme climate events by 2050 and more than 50% of all biosphere reserves overlap with another international designation.
India’s Biosphere Reserves
India is at the forefront of promoting and managing Biosphere Reserves, showcasing its dedication to conserving biodiversity and advancing sustainable ecosystem practices.
India’s Biosphere Reserve Network
India’s Biosphere Reserve network represents its varied ecosystems and diverse ecological heritage. As per the Ministry of Environment Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), the country has
18 notified Biosphere Reserves
, of which
13 belong to UNESCO’s World Network of Biosphere Reserve
s. This represents the highest number of internationally recognised biosphere reserves in South Asia.

Alongside this growing network, India has put in place a dedicated programme to manage and conserve these ecologically significant areas. The
Biosphere Reserve
division of the Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change administers a Centrally Sponsored Scheme namely
'Biodiversity Conservation' scheme,
which is a sub­-scheme under umbrella scheme
'Conservation of Natural Resources and Eco­systems'
.
Under the scheme, the Division supports Biosphere Reserves (designated under framework of UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme) by providing grants­-in -aid to the States where the Biosphere Reserves are located, for conservation and development activities as specified in their Management Plan. The implementation of this scheme is undertaken by the State Forest Departments. Thus,
the Ministry provides grants­ in ­aid to the states on cost sharing basis i.e. 60:40 (Central: State) for other States and 90:10 (Central: State) to North Eastern and Himalayan States.
Since 2022–23, the Ministry has piloted five-year Integrated Management Plans for four reserves:
Nanda Devi (Uttarakhand), Pachmarhi (Madhya Pradesh), Dehang-Dibang (Arunachal Pradesh) and Agasthyamalai (Kerala & Tamil Nadu).
These plans bring reserve authorities, research institutions and local communities together. Their priorities include habitat restoration, biodiversity monitoring, scientific research and sustainable livelihoods.

A Glimpse into India’s Biosphere Reserves
From mountain forests to mangrove deltas, coral reefs and high-altitude deserts, India’s Biosphere Reserves harbour extraordinary life.
Nilgiri:
Located within the Western Ghats, the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve is a globally significant biodiversity hotspot. Spanning approximately 5,52,000 hectares across Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka, it encompasses tropical evergreen forests, montane shola forests and grasslands. This diverse landscape supports rich biodiversity, including endemic and threatened species. The reserve harbours the endangered lion-tailed macaque and Nilgiri tahr, alongside elephants, tigers, gaur, sambar and chital. It supports more than 100 mammal species and 550 bird species, besides numerous reptiles and amphibians. The Nilgiri district alone records over 6,000 plant species, highlighting the region's exceptional botanical wealth.
Cold Desert:
The Cold Desert Biosphere Reserve in Himachal Pradesh spans 7,770 square kilometres at elevations of 3,300–6,600 metres. Its harsh, high-altitude landscape supports 732 vascular plant species, including 30 endemics, alongside snow leopards, Himalayan ibex, and blue sheep. Around 12,000 people inhabit the region, sustaining traditional livelihoods through pastoralism, yak and goat herding, barley and pea farming, and Tibetan herbal medicine.
Gulf of Mannar:
The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve, located off the southeastern coast of Tamil Nadu, is one of India’s richest marine biodiversity regions.  Spanning approximately 1.05 million hectares, it also encompasses coral reefs, seagrass beds and mangroves. These interconnected ecosystems support 4,223 plant and animal species. The reserve sustains around 25 lakh people across a region with approximately 47 coastal villages.
Success Story: People at the Heart of Conservation
The indigenous communities in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve turn uprooted Lantana vines into elephant sculptures, furniture, and crafts.
This initiative supports local livelihoods while raising awareness about habitat degradation.
In 2021, 125 life-sized Lantana elephants were displayed in London, promoting wildlife coexistence
. Sculptures have also appeared at Bengaluru Airport, across Bengaluru, and at
Rashtrapati Bhavan
. The initiative gives removed Lantana an economic use, creates livelihood opportunities for Indigenous artisans and raises public awareness of invasive species.
Did You Know?
Lantana camara is an invasive shrub that has spread across approximately 300,000 square kilometres of Indian forests. It forms dense thickets that suppress native plants, reduce biodiversity, and alter natural fire patterns. Its chemical secretions inhibit the growth of competing vegetation, while its rapid regrowth makes removal difficult. Despite eradication efforts since 1916, controlling Lantana remains costly and challenging.
The Way Forward
India’s Biosphere Reserves offer a promising model for a future where nature and people thrive together. Continued investment in scientific research, habitat restoration and community-led conservation can preserve their ecological richness. By combining traditional knowledge with modern monitoring, India can support resilient ecosystems and sustainable livelihoods. Strong partnerships among governments, researchers, local communities and international organisations will help these landscapes flourish. Ultimately, Biosphere Reserves can demonstrate how protecting nature also enriches lives, safeguards cultural heritage and secures a healthier future for generations to come.

content:
The intense heat in the Earth's interior is a powerful source of clean energy called geothermal energy. Given India's rich geothermal resources, this form of energy holds immense promise as a round-the-clock available source of power. The National Policy on Geothermal Energy aims to harness this potential. It seeks to make geothermal energy a key part of the nation's renewable energy story as India drives towards Net Zero by 2070. The recent commissioning of the first two geothermal wells in Ladakh marks the beginning of this journey.
Harnessing Geothermal Energy for a Sustainable India
Deep below the Earth's surface, emanating from the intense heat of its interior, lies a constant, low-carbon source of energy called geothermal energy. In locations with suitable geology and tectonics, this energy can be tapped to generate power or used directly on the ground. Unlike solar and wind energy, this source provides renewable energy that is available round the clock. Recognising this potential, the Government notified the
National Policy on Geothermal Energy
in September 2025. The policy charts a clear roadmap for exploring and developing India's geothermal resources. The
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE)
is the nodal ministry for its implementation.
Building on this framework, India achieved a historic milestone in July 2026. The ONGC Energy Centre commissioned the country's
first two geothermal wells in Puga Valley, Ladakh
. At a height of over 14,000 feet above sea level, Puga Valley is among India's most promising geothermal sites, known for its hot springs and underground heat reserves. The two 1,000-metre-deep wells will support reservoir evaluation. They also pave the way for
India's first 1-megawatt demonstration geothermal power project
, marking the country's entry into geothermal power generation.
As India advances its clean energy transition, geothermal power offers a dependable, indigenous way to diversify the nation's renewable energy mix.

Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo (Bharat RE) 2026
is being held from
2–5 November 2026
at

‘Invest. Innovate. Inspire.

are participating, showcasing renewable energy potential, investment opportunities, and clean manufacturing capabilities. Key focus areas of the summit include solar and wind energy, green hydrogen, energy storage, grid integration, domestic manufacturing, digitalisation and artificial intelligence applications in the energy sector. The Summit provides a global platform for clean energy investment, technology partnerships and industry collaboration. It features ministerial discussions, CEO roundtables, investor engagements and an exhibition featuring
over 400 exhibitors
. The event is being held alongside the

and the

strengthening international cooperation across the clean energy sector.[1]

Understanding Geothermal Energy: An Overview
Geothermal Energy is
a steady, low-carbon and weather-independent energy source.It holds a vast untapped resource base to strengthen India's clean energy future and cut reliance on fossil fuels.
Formation of Geothermal Energy
The Earth's interior consists of four main layers: the outermost, solid crust;the middle, semi-solid mantle; and the core divided into a dense liquid outer core and solid inner core. The temperature of the interior rises with depth - the mantle temperature reaches about 3700Celsius degrees at its boundary with the core, while the core temperature goes up to 5000- 6000 Celsius.This heat is generated by radioactive decay of elements like uranium, thorium, and potassium, as well as residual heat left over from the planet's formation.  This heat gives rise to huge convection currents in the mantle, as hot material moves up from the core boundary towards the cooler, upper parts of the mantle and crust. This material also contains water trapped as hydroxides.  These convection currents give rise to all tectonic activity, including earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain building. In geologically active regions, faults and fractures let the hot material travel closer to the surface.This process creates reservoirs of hot water and steam, trapped within permeable rock. This thermal energy, harnessed from within the Earth, is known as geothermal energy
.
From Geothermal Energy to Power Production
Geothermal power generation converts the earth's natural heat into electricity by tapping hot water and
steam trapped beneath the surface.Deep wells bring these resources up to the surface. The steam then drives a turbine connected to a generator. This process resembles conventional thermal power generation
. However, it replaces fuel combustion with naturally occurring underground heat. After power generation, the used water is condensed and reinjected into the reservoir. This supports resource replenishment and enables continued energy production.Geothermal energy also supports direct heat applications across district heating, agriculture, aquaculture, and space heating &cooling, enabling efficient utilisation of geothermal heat.
Inside the Earth
From the centre outward, the Earth is structured in four distinct layers. The
inner core
is a solid ball of iron and nickel, about 2,400 km wide. The
outer core
surrounding it is a liquid layer of molten iron and nickel, roughly 2,400 km thick. The
mantle
, composed mostly of hot, dense rock, extends nearly 2,900 km and forms the largest layer. Finally, the
crust
is the thin, solid outer layer, ranging from about 5 to 8 kilometres thick beneath the oceans to 24 to 56 kilometres thick beneath the continents.
India's Geothermal Resource Base
India's varied geology offers a strong foundation for geothermal development. The Geological Survey of India (GSI) has mapped
381 hot springs and identified 10 geothermal provinces nationwide
. India's theoretical geothermal prospect stands at nearly 10.6 GW. Of this,
42 sites have been recognised as promising for power generation and direct heat use.
The 10 geothermal provinces include the Himalayan Geothermal Province, Naga-Lusai, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Son Narmada Tapi (SONATA), West Coast, Cambay Graben, Aravalli, Mahanadi, Godavari, and South Indian Cratonic regions.
India's geothermal rift basins hold strong scope, owing to favourable geology and tectonics. But suitable projects can arise anywhere geothermal resources exist. Advanced technologies like
Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS)
and
Advanced Geothermal Systems (AGS)
will further widen exploration opportunities.
Repurposing Abandoned Oil and Gas Wells
Geothermal energy can be extracted from abandoned oil and gas wells.Inactive or unproductive wells can potentially be repurposed for geothermal initiatives, subject to technical and operational feasibility. This approach builds on existing drilling expertise, well data and infrastructure from the oil and gas sector.
India’s Geothermal Expansion
India is moving from resource assessment to field demonstration with remarkable speed. This momentum is reflected in the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy sanctioning five research and development projects between July and August 2025, covering resource assessment, indigenous technology development and field demonstration. The projects span electricity generation, heating and cooling applications. These efforts are generating the technical data and field experience needed for future commercial deployment.

Significant geothermal resources, advancing technologies and early field activity are laying the foundation for a future of geothermal energy in India. While commercial-scale power generation is yet to be established, expanding well fields, demonstration activities and research and development initiatives are strengthening the ecosystem for wider deployment.
Unlocking India’s Geothermal Potential: Policy & Partnerships
Geothermal energy is a proven, established renewable technology worldwide.
Global installed capacity reached 15.67 GW by the end of 2025
. Indonesia, the US, the Philippines, Türkiye and New Zealand lead the field, together holding around 67% of global capacity. India is now building a strong ecosystem to advance geothermal energy from resource assessment to real-world deployment. National programmes and international partnerships are driving this mission forward, powering research, technology development and knowledge exchange across the sector.
National Policy on Geothermal Energy, 2025
The National Policy on Geothermal Energy aims to establish geothermal energy as a major renewable pillar. It promotes systematic exploration and deployment of India's geothermal resources. The Policy prioritises research, drilling, reservoir management, and direct-use applications. It also supports Ground Source Heat Pumps (GSHPs) for heating and cooling. A clear regulatory framework encourages both public and private sector participation. The Policy facilitates repurposing abandoned oil and gas wells for geothermal use. It further supports a national geothermal data repository, pilot projects, and Centres of Excellence.
Renewable Energy Research and Technology Development Programme (RE-RTD)
MNRE is implementing the RE-RTD scheme through research institutions and industry partners. This initiative aims to develop indigenous, cost-effective technologies for renewable energy, including geothermal energy, across the country.
International Collaborations
India has advanced its geothermal energy efforts through collaborations with several international partners. Under cooperation mechanisms with
Australia
and
Iceland
, geothermal energy has been identified as a key area of cooperation. Similarly, an MoU with the
Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
designated geothermal energy as a focus area of bilateral engagement.
These initiatives are providing a coordinated platform for translating India’s geothermal resources into scalable solutions across sectors.
New Dimension in India’s Renewable Energy Mix
India's geothermal energy journey reflects the Government's steadfast commitment to energy security and sustainable growth. From notifying the National Policy on Geothermal Energy to commissioning the country's first two geothermal wells at Puga Valley, Ladakh, India has moved decisively from planning to implementation. The country holds a theoretical geothermal resource potential of nearly 10,600 MW. Growing pilot projects and strengthening international collaborations are expanding its applications, from power generation to heating, geo-tourism and agriculture. Geothermal energy is thus emerging as a valuable addition to India's renewable energy portfolio. As India advances towards its 2070 Net Zero target, geothermal energy will remain a steady, indigenous pillar of the country's energy transition and progress.

content:
As clean energy reshapes India's power landscape, a timeless technology is paving the way for a powerful new energy future. Often described as a water battery, pumped storage uses water and gravity to store electricity, bridging the gap between when power is generated and when it is needed. From reservoirs to modern grids, it is helping shape a cleaner, more reliable and resilient energy future.
Building India's Energy Future with Storage
India’s energy transition is increasingly anchored in renewable energy to strengthen energy security and sustainability. The country is rapidly expanding solar and wind capacity to meet rising electricity demand with cleaner sources. As of September 2026, India has 308.027 GW of installed non-fossil fuel-based electricity generation capacity. During FY 2025–26, India added around 55.29 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity. India has also set a target of 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030. Solar and wind energy are going to make major contributions towards achieving this target
.
However, renewable energy generation varies with sunlight, weather and daily demand patterns. This variability creates a growing need to store electricity when renewable generation exceeds demand. Energy storage can then supply electricity during periods of low renewable generation or peak demand.
As renewable capacity expands, the requirement for energy storage would also increase rapidly. The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) projects 73.93 GW of storage capacity by 2031–32. This includes 26.69 GW from Pumped Storage Projects (PSPs) and 47.24 GW from Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS).
PSPs can play a crucial role in meeting this long-duration storage requirement. PSPs store electricity by pumping water to an upper reservoir during periods of surplus generation. The stored water is released through turbines when electricity demand rises. This enables PSPs to shift renewable electricity across time and support grid stability. They also provide long-duration storage and peaking support, making them important for integrating large renewable capacities.
Types of Energy Storage
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and Pumped Storage Projects (PSPs) offer complementary solutions for integrating renewable energy into the grid.
BESS can respond rapidly to short-duration requirements
,
supporting frequency regulation, peak management and grid balancing. PSPs provide
long-duration storage
, shifting large quantities of electricity across periods of surplus and demand. BESS can be deployed relatively quickly and close to renewable generation or consumption centres. PSPs require suitable geographical conditions but can provide large-scale storage over extended periods. Their long operating life also supports sustained grid infrastructure needs.

Understanding PSPs: Cycle of Energy Storage and Supply
A Pumped Storage Project typically consists of two reservoirs located at different elevations. During periods of surplus electricity, water is pumped from the lower reservoir to the upper reservoir, where energy is stored as potential energy. When electricity is required, water is released from the upper reservoir through turbines to generate electricity. Once demand subsides, water is pumped back to the upper reservoir during periods of surplus electricity, completing the storage cycle. Pumped Storage Projects therefore function as large-scale energy storage systems and contribute to grid stability and renewable energy integration.
Categorising Pumped Storage Power Plants
PSPs are classified according to how their reservoirs are connected to, or situated in relation to, natural watercourses. They are grouped into three types:
on-stream, off-stream open-loop and off-stream closed-loop schemes
. These configurations reflect the varying association between a project’s reservoirs and natural watercourses.
On-stream Pumped Storage
On-stream pumped storage schemeshave
both reservoirs located on a river, stream or nallah.
To meet the electricity demands, water stored in the upper reservoir flows through turbines to generate electricity. During periods of low electricity demand or surplus power, water is pumped back to the upper reservoir for reuse.
Off-stream Open-loop Pumped Storage
Off-stream open-loop pumped storage schemes have
one reservoir located on a river, stream or nallah. In contrast, the other reservoir is not located on a river, a perennial stream, or a perennial nallah
. When electricity is required, water flows from the upper reservoir through turbines to produce electricity. Surplus electricity is subsequently used to pump the water back, restoring the system for another cycle.
Off-stream Closed-loop Pumped Storage
Neither reservoir in an off-stream closed-loop pumped storage scheme is located on a river, perennial stream or perennial nallah.
Both reservoirs are situated away from perennial natural watercourses. When electricity is required, water flows from the upper reservoir through turbines that generate power, and is then pumped back to the upper reservoir during periods of low electricity demand or surplus power.
All three types of Pumped StorageProjects have a role based on site-specific geographical and technical conditions.However, efforts are being made to identify more off-stream projects located away from rivers, supporting faster project execution and minimising impacts on aquatic ecology and the surrounding environment.
Scaling Up Energy Storage: India's Pumped Storage Momentum
India is rapidly expanding its pumped storage capacity to support its growing renewable energy base. The development is progressing across operational, construction and pre-construction stages. This expanding pipeline is strengthening India’s long-duration energy storage infrastructure.

India's Regionally Diverse Pumped Storage Potential
India has identified 320 pumped storage projects with a combined potential of 345.38 GW. This includes 62 on-stream projects with 56.67 GW and 258 off-stream projects with 288.71 GW. These projects span all five regions and include different stages of development,
including projects already in operation
.
PSP development and site suitability require assessment of several technical and environmental aspects. These include topography, geology, hydrology, reservoir characteristics, foundation conditions, seismicity and environmental considerations. Construction materials, power potential and transmission connectivity are also examined during project appraisal.
The Western Region has the highest identified potential at 129.72 GW. CEA attributes this mainly to topographical features and steep gradients of rivers originating from the Western Ghats.

This extensive resource base provides a strong foundation for scaling long-duration energy storage. The Central Electricity Authority has therefore mapped a substantial capacity addition pathway through 2035–36.
Projects totalling 100.81 GW are envisaged for commissioning by 2035–36.
This includes projects already under construction and would take cumulative PSP capacity to 105.56 GW. Government Initiatives and Measures
The Government of India has taken a series of coordinated policy, regulatory, demand-side and supply-side measures to promote the development and deployment of PSPs.
Dedicated PSP Development Guidelines:
The Ministry of Power notified the
Guidelines to Promote Development of Pumped Storage Projects in India
in April 2023.
The guidelines provide a policy framework for facilitating faster PSP development.

Support for Enabling Infrastructure:
Budgetary support covers essential infrastructure required for PSP development. This includes roads, bridges, railway sidings, ropeways, communication facilities and transmission lines. These measures improve project connectivity and strengthen project viability.
Competitive Procurement Framework:
Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) Guidelines were notified in February 2025. They provide a transparent and standardised framework for procuring storage capacity and stored energy from PSPs.
Inter-State Transmission System Charge Waiver:
PSPs awarded for construction by 30 June 2028 are eligible for a 100% ISTS charge waiver. The waiver applies for 25 years from commercial operation. This measure strengthens the financial viability of PSPs.
Faster Project Approvals:
Revised CEA guidelines have reduced Detailed Project Report concurrence timelines. The timeline has been reduced from 90 days to 50 days for all PSPs. The requirement for clearance of Inter-State Aspects has also been removed. These measures support faster project development.
Streamlined Environmental Appraisal:
The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has introduced differentiated appraisal provisions for PSPs. Eligible projects can benefit from B2 categorisation under the applicable provisions. Off-stream projects also benefit from reduced baseline data requirements. These measures can accelerate environmental appraisal while maintaining regulatory safeguards.
Facilitating Survey and Investigation:
MoEF&CC extended forest land survey provisions and enhanced borehole exploration limits for PSPs, facilitating timely preparation of technically robust Detailed Project Reports.
Integrated Grid and Transmission Planning:
National electricity planning integrates energy storage and transmission development. This approach addresses renewable energy variability, reduces congestion and strengthens grid reliability. A roadmap envisages integrating 100 GW of PSP capacity between 2025–26 and 2035–36.
Digital Project Monitoring:
The Central Electricity Authority’s Jal Vidyut DPR portal enables real-time monitoring of survey and investigation activities. It also facilitates coordination among stakeholders during project preparation. This digital approach helps streamline approvals and accelerate PSP development.
Review of limit of capital expenditure requiring the concurrence of the CEA:
Government of India, vide Gazette Notification dated 01.08.2025, has revised the capital expenditure limit for schemes related to setting up hydro generating stations to ₹3,000 crore, requiring the concurrence of the CEA. Further, off-stream closed-loop pumped storage schemes, irrespective of the quantum of capital expenditure have been exempted from the requirement of concurrence by the CEA
These measures spanning policy clarity, fiscal support, streamlined clearances, competitive procurement and integrated grid planning have created an enabling environment for the accelerated development of PSPs.
Energy Transition's Next Imperative
India's target of achieving 500 Gigawatts of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030 represents a fundamental shift in the country's electricity landscape. As renewable energy assumes a larger role, the ability to store energy and deploy it in line with demand will become increasingly important for maintaining a reliable and balanced power system. Pumped Storage Hydropower is well positioned to address this requirement through its ability to provide large-scale, long-duration energy storage while supporting a range of wider power system needs. Its role extends from managing peak demand and integrating variable renewable energy to strengthening grid flexibility and resilience.As the clean energy ecosystem continues to evolve, the effective deployment of energy storage alongside generation and transmission infrastructure will be central to building a power system that is cleaner, more flexible and prepared for the future.
