content:
Green hydrogen is emerging as a pillar of India’s clean energy transition. It is produced by splitting water using renewable electricity. It can help reduce emissions in sectors such as fertiliser production, petroleum refining, iron and steel manufacturing, heavy-duty road transport and shipping
.
The National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM) supports domestic manufacturing, production, assured demand and credible certification. From green ammonia auctions to India’s first hydrogen train, early projects point to a promising path.
Why Green Hydrogen
Hydrogen is an energy carrier that stores energy and delivers it for varied uses. In a fuel cell, it reacts with oxygen to produce electricity, leaving only water and heat as by-products, and no polluting compounds or greenhouse gases.Although pure hydrogen is not found in large quantities in nature, it can be extracted from compounds such as water or natural gas. Its environmental impact therefore depends on how it is made. Conventional methods rely on fossil fuels and release carbon emissions.
Production using renewable electricity from solar and wind power can cut this footprint substantially. Hydrogen made by splitting water using renewable power is called
green hydrogen
. Unlike fossil-based routes, this process emits far less carbon. India’s abundant solar and wind resources make domestic production feasible. This diversifies the country’s energy sources and strengthens energy security.
It also supports India’s goal of net-zero emissions by 2070.Green hydrogen matters most in sectors where cutting emissions is difficult. Reasons include high-temperature heat needs, chemical processes and few alternatives to fossil fuels.
These hard-to-abate sectors
include fertiliser, petroleum refining, iron and steel, heavy-duty road transport and shipping. Fertiliser and refining plants already use hydrogen, so green hydrogen can replace the fossil-based supply. It can also support lower-emission steelmaking, selected transport uses and energy storage. It is especially useful where direct electrification is difficult or less practical.
What Makes Hydrogen “Green”
Hydrogen releases no carbon dioxide when used, so its climate impact depends on how it is produced. In August 2023, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) notified India’s Green Hydrogen Standard. Hydrogen qualifies as green if emissions do not exceed 2 kg of CO₂ equivalent per kg of hydrogen, on a well-to-gate basis, measured as a 12-month average. India thus became one of the first few countries to define green hydrogen formally.
For India, wider adoption could reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels. It would also lessen exposure to global fuel price swings. The sector could open opportunities in manufacturing, draw investment, create jobs and expand exports. Building capabilities across the value chain would strengthen domestic supply chains and spur industrial innovation. Green hydrogen can thus support self-reliance, sustainable industrial growth and a low-carbon future.

How Is Green Hydrogen Produced?
Green hydrogen is produced mainly through water (H₂O) electrolysis. Electrolysis uses electricity to split a compound into simpler substances. Here, renewable electricity splits water into hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂), with minimal emissions.
2H2O
→
2H2   +   O2
The key equipment is the
electrolyser.
It contains
two electrodes
, a cathode and an anode, connected to a power source. They operate within an
electrolyte,
which helps ions move through the cell. A
diaphragm
keeps the gases apart while allowing ions to pass. When
current flows
, hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. The gases are collected separately for further usage. An electrolyser thus turns renewable electricity and water into a low-emission fuel for industry, transport and other uses.
Did You Know?
Water is purified before electrolysis, because impurities can damage cells and shorten their life. According to MNRE, about nine litres of demineralised water is needed per kg of hydrogen. Afterwards, the hydrogen is dried and purified before compression. India’s Green Hydrogen Standard counts emissions from each of these steps.
Applications of Green Hydrogen
Fertilisers:
Ammonia, made from hydrogen and nitrogen, is the base for nitrogen fertilisers such as urea. Most of this hydrogen now comes from natural gas. Green hydrogen can replace it and yield green ammonia with far lower emissions.
Petroleum refineries:
Refineries use hydrogen to remove sulphur from petrol and diesel, so the fuels burn cleaner. They also use it to upgrade heavy oil into lighter fuels such as diesel, aviation turbine fuel and naphtha. These fuels serve road transport, aviation and industry. Most refinery hydrogen comes from fossil fuels, so a green supply can cut refining emissions.
Steel:
Conventional steelmaking uses coal to strip oxygen from iron ore, releasing carbon dioxide. In direct reduced iron routes, green hydrogen can do this job instead. The reduction stage then releases water vapour in place of carbon dioxide.
City gas networks:
Green hydrogen can be blended with natural gas in limited proportions, subject to safety standards and infrastructure compatibility. This allows existing gas networks to supply a hydrogen-natural gas blend to homes, businesses and industries. Such blending can reduce fossil fuel consumption and associated emissions while utilising existing distribution infrastructure.
Road and rail transport:
Fuel-cell vehicles convert hydrogen into electricity on board, which drives electric motors. Their only emission at the point of use is water vapour. This suits buses, trucks and trains that need long range and quick refuelling.
Did You Know?
India’s first indigenous hydrogen-powered train was inaugurated on 17 July 2026 on the Jind–Sonipat section. The 10-car trainset can carry around 2,600 passengers. A facility at Jind stores nearly 3,000 kg of hydrogen. The train emits only water vapour and heat. Click to
Read More
Shipping:
Green hydrogen can be converted into green ammonia and green methanol, which can fuel ships. These can replace conventional marine fuels on long voyages. Adoption depends on engine compatibility, safety requirements and port infrastructure.
Exports:
India can supply green hydrogen and derivatives, such as green ammonia and green methanol, to countries seeking low-emission fuels. India’s renewable energy resources can support this supply. Exports can open industrial opportunities and strengthen India’s position in low-emission fuels.
Click to Read:
India’s Green Hydrogen Production Potential
Bringing Cohesion in Government Approach
The Government has adopted an integrated strategy to increase the adoption of Green hydrogen across the sector. It coordinates with Central and State Ministries, Departments, agencies and institutions to drive adoption. Each Ministry has a defined role. For example, the
Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas
promotes use in refineries and city gas distribution; the
Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers
encourage indigenous green ammonia-based fertilisers; the
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
enable transport use through regulations, standards and codes; the
Ministry of Steel
drives adoption in steelmaking; the
Ministry of External Affairs
facilitates collaboration with global partners.
India’s Green Hydrogen Policy Architecture
NGHM: A mission for the whole ecosystem
MNRE is implementing the NGHM to make India a global hub for green hydrogen and its derivatives. The Union Cabinet approved the Mission in January 2023 with an outlay of Rs. 19,744 crore. It targets production capacity of at least 5 million metric tonnes (MMT) annually by 2030. With export demand, this could reach 10 MMT per year. The Mission has the following components.
SIGHT: Support on both sides of the market
The
Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition (SIGHT)
Programme is a key NGHM component. Its outlay is Rs.17,490 crore up to 2029–30. It offers incentives for two purposes: domestic electrolyser manufacturing and green hydrogen production. Together, they strengthen indigenous capability and speed up production.
Key Progress
Incentives have been awarded to 15 companies for 3,000 MW per annum of electrolyser manufacturing capacity. This reduces dependence on imported supply chains.
About 8,000 tonnes per annum of green hydrogen capacity had been commissioned by February 2026.
Incentives have been awarded for 8,62,000 tonnes per annum of green hydrogen production capacity.
Till October 2026, Indian companies have signed the world's largest Green Hydrogen offtake commitments - totalling
over 5.5 lakh MTPA
-positioning India as the global leader in Green Hydrogen supply commitments.[2]
Pilot Projects
The NGHM supports pilots that replace fossil fuels and feedstocks in hard-to-abate sectors. These include steel, heavy-duty mobility and shipping. The pilots aim to identify technological, regulatory and infrastructure gaps.They will also test supply chains and technology integration. Their findings will guide commercial-scale deployment and the policy support needed. The Mission has earmarked Rs. 455 crore for low-carbon steel up to 2029–30. It has also earmarked Rs. 496 crore for mobility and Rs.115 crore for shipping up to 2025–26.
Key Progress
Five pilot projects have been sanctioned in the steel sector. Rs.84 crore is sanctioned for testing 100% hydrogen injection.
Twelve projects will deploy 70 hydrogen vehicles: 27 buses and 43 trucks. These include fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) and hydrogen internal combustion engine (H₂-ICE) vehicles.
The projects also cover 16 hydrogen refuelling stations across 21 routes. Financial assistance of Rs. 41.58 crore has been released.
V.O. Chidambaranar Port Authority has awarded a pilot project to develop bunkering and refuelling facilities for green methanol. The project costs Rs. 38.12 crore, including an MNRE grant of Rs. 35 crore.
Green Hydrogen Hubs and
Hydrogen Valley Innovation Clusters (HVIC)
Hydrogen is difficult to transport. To address this, the Mission promotes hubs and HVICs. This cluster approach brings production, consumption and infrastructure together. It improves project viability and enables economies of scale. Projects in designated hubs can also access Central and State scheme benefits. The Mission has an outlay of Rs.400 crore up to 2025–26 for hubs and related projects. These initiatives aim to attract green investment and accelerate innovation.
Key Progress
MNRE has recognised Deendayal Port (Kandla, Gujarat), V.O. Chidambaranar Port (Tuticorin, Tamil Nadu) and Paradip Port (Odisha) as hubs.
An indigenously built 1 MW green hydrogen plant was commissioned at Kandla Port in July 2025.
Four HVICs have been awarded: Jodhpur, Odisha, Pune and Kerala.
Enabling Policy Framework
The Mission follows a whole-of-government approach to make green hydrogen affordable. MNRE coordinates with Central and State departments on benefits and project facilitation. Key measures include waiving interstate transmission charges and facilitating renewable energy banking. They also include time-bound Open Access and grid connectivity. The Government will coordinate planning for renewable capacity, transmission, banking and storage. Solar Parks, Manufacturing Zones and Special Economic Zones (SEZs) may be extended to hydrogen facilities. The Mission will also explore international green finance, green bonds and innovative financing.
Key Progress
Green hydrogen and green ammonia plants commissioned by 31 December 2030 are
exempt fromInter-State Transmission System (ISTS)
charges for 25 years. ISTS are fees for moving power across state boundaries. The waiver lowers electricity costs.
The
Green Energy Corridor Scheme
supports lines and substations that carry renewable power to the grid. A national transmission plan improves links between generation and consumption centres.
Click to Read More
Duty benefits
under Section 26 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, have been extended to eligible units installing and operating renewable energy equipment exclusively for captive consumption. This can reduce the cost of setting up renewable energy facilities within SEZs to meet their own electricity requirements.
Standalone plants producing green hydrogen or green ammonia through water electrolysis using renewable energy have been
exempted from prior Environmental Clearance
under the Environment Impact Assessment Notification, 2006. This can simplify the approval process for eligible projects.
Renewable energy plants located within a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) or Export Oriented Unit (EOU) are
exempt from the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) and Revised List of Models and Manufacturers (RLMM) requirements
when supplying electricity exclusively to green hydrogen production plants or their derivatives. This provides eligible projects greater flexibility in sourcing renewable energy equipment, subject to the applicable exemption conditions.
The Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia Policy provides for
Open Access within 15 days
and
banking of surplus renewable electricity for up to 30 days
, subject to applicable provisions. Open Access allows producers to procure renewable electricity from sources other than their local distribution company. Banking allows surplus electricity to be stored as a credit and used later, subject to applicable regulations.
Hydrogen Storage and Safety
Hydrogen is the lightest element and burns easily[3], so storage, handling and leak detection need strict standards[4].India has notified standards for green hydrogen, green ammonia and green methanol to guide safe industry practice[5].
Regulations and Standards
The Mission is building regulations and standards aligned with industry needs. The aim is to enable sector growth and harmonise with international norms.
Key Progress
India’s Green Hydrogen Standard has been notified. It sets a ceiling of 2 kg CO₂ equivalent per kg of hydrogen, well-to-gate, averaged over a 12-month period. This created a common benchmark.
Scheme guidelines have been issued to fund testing facilities, infrastructure and institutional support for standards.
Standards for green ammonia and green methanol have been notified. They set emission thresholds and eligibility conditions, supporting production and trade.
MNRE launched the
Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme
of India in April 2025.The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) accredits agencies for monitoring, verification and certification.
A dedicated portal went live in June 2026 for transparent certification and compliance. Credible certification will help Indian producers compete with confidence globally.
Research and Development
The Mission supports research and development (R&D) to make green hydrogen more affordable, efficient, safe and reliable. The Strategic Hydrogen Innovation Partnership (SHIP) is a public-private framework, with a dedicated R&D fund from industry and Government. Scheme guidelines for R&D were notified in March 2024, with an outlay of Rs. 400 crore. As of June 2026, an initial R&D roadmap worth Rs. 113 crore is supporting approved projectsacross hydrogen production, storage, and safety technologies.
Skilling
A coordinated skill development initiative is under way. The Mission aims to generate over 6 lakh jobs across the value chain by 2030. So far, 8,149 candidates have been trained and 7,248 certified in hydrogen-related qualifications across 14 States and Union Territories. Training spans renewable power for electrolysers, electrolysis, storage, transport, safety standards and end usesuch as steel, mobility and refining. For innovation, Rs.100 crore has been allocated to start-ups working on green hydrogen technologies. The first nine start-ups have been approved, with total funding of Rs. 22 crore.
International Cooperation
The Mission promotes partnerships to develop technology, mobilise investment, build export markets and align standards.
Key Progress
MNRE, directly or through the National Institute of Solar Energy, has signed MoUs, Letters of Intent or Joint Declarations of Intent. The partners are Australia, Finland, France, Germany, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Uzbekistan.
An MoU on renewable energy has been signed with the Netherlands.
An India–US Hydrogen Task Force has been formed under the Strategic Clean Energy Partnership.
Green hydrogen is a focus area of the India–US New and Emerging Renewable Energy Technology Action Platform (RETAP).
State-level Initiatives
Six States have notified dedicated green hydrogen policies, complementing the National Green Hydrogen Mission.
Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and West Bengal
are the States with notified dedicated policies.
Four more States are finalising their dedicated green hydrogen policies. Haryana, Punjab, Bihar and Keralam are working on the draft policies.
Seven States have integrated hydrogen into their existing industrial and renewable energy policy frameworks.These includeHimachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Telangana and Chhattisgarh.
The Road Ahead
The National Green Hydrogen Mission marks an important step towards building a cleaner, more self-reliant and globally competitive energy economy. By 2030, India aims to develop
5 million metric tonnes (MMT) of annual green hydrogen production capacity
. This transition can reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthen the country’s long-term energy security. The Mission is expected to reduce cumulative fossil fuel imports by approximately
Rs. 1 lakh crore by 2030
.
Beyond energy security, the Mission seeks to create new opportunities for industrial growth, investment and employment. It is expected to mobilise over
Rs. 8 lakh crore in investments
and generate more than
6 lakh jobs
across manufacturing, infrastructure, research and project development. The production and use of the targeted green hydrogen quantum could also help avert nearly
50 MMT of carbon dioxide emissions annually
. Through these efforts, the Government aims to accelerate industrial decarbonisation, strengthen domestic manufacturing and position India as a global hub for green hydrogen production, use and exports. This will contribute to India’s broader vision of
Viksit Bharat by 2047
and its commitment to achieving
net-zero emissions by 2070
.

content:
At the intersection of agriculture and renewable energy lies an innovative approach to making farmland more productive. Agrivoltaics combines crop cultivation with solar power generation on the same land, enabling farmers to diversify their incomes while contributing to India’s clean energy transition. By bringing food production and solar electricity together, it offers a promising pathway towards efficient land use, greater farm resilience and sustainable rural prosperity.
Solar Power for Agri Farms and a Cleaner Future
Agriculture plays a vital role in India’s economy, serving as a key source of livelihood for approximately 46.1 per cent of the population. The Gross Value Added (GVA) of the Agriculture and Allied Sector is estimated to reach
Rs. 52.08 lakh crore in 2025-26
. Sustaining this vital sector requires reliable and affordable energy for irrigation and other farming operations. Solar power can help meet these everyday needs while advancing India’s clean energy transition.
Click to Read More: The New Era of Indian Agriculture and Allied Sectors
India’s vast agricultural land offers significant prospects to integrate solar energy with farming. According to
Land Use Statistics for 2023-24
, the country’s reported area covers
306.96 million hectares
, of which approximately
55 per cent is agricultural land
. The
net sown area stands at 138.99 million hectares
, while the
gross cropped area covers 217.88 million hectares
. This extensive land base offers opportunities to generate solar electricity alongside agricultural production. Farmers can use solar power to operate
irrigation pumps, reduce dependence on conventional electricity and potentially supplementary revenue
by supplying surplus electricity to the grid. For instance, solar-powered irrigation pumps can provide daytime power for watering crops while reducing reliance on diesel-powered alternatives.
Agrivoltaics takes this integration further by bringing together crop cultivation and solar electricity generation on the same land.
Solar panels installed above or between crop rows allow electricity generation alongside continued farming. Depending on the crop, panel design and local conditions, partial shading may also help reduce soil moisture loss. This approach can improve land-use efficiency, diversify farm earnings and strengthening both food and energy security. Through research, field demonstrations and policy development, India is exploring ways to adapt agrivoltaics to diverse agricultural conditions. It offers a promising pathway to align farmers’ livelihoods with India’s wider renewable energy ambitions.
The
Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo (Bharat RE) 2026
is being held from
2–5 November 2026
at
Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi
, under the theme
‘Invest. Innovate. Inspire.
’ The four-day Summit brings together participants from over 130 countries, including more than
40 Ministers
,
policymakers
,
investors
,
financial institutions
and
industry leaders
.
Nine Countries-
Australia, Denmark, the European Union, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom will participate as Country Partners.
13 Indian States and Union Territories
are participating, showcasing renewable energy potential, investment opportunities, and clean manufacturing capabilities. Key focus areas of the summit includes solar and wind energy, green hydrogen, energy storage, grid integration, domestic manufacturing, digitalisation and artificial intelligence applications in the energy sector. The Summit provides a global platform for clean energy investment, technology partnerships and industry collaboration. It features ministerial discussions, CEO roundtables, investor engagements and an exhibition featuring
over 400 exhibitors
. The event is being held alongside the
9th International Solar Alliance Assembly
and the
4th International Conference on Green Hydrogen,
strengthening international cooperation across the clean energy sector.

Agrivoltaics: Bridging Agriculture and Renewable Energy
Agrivoltaics, also known as
agrisolar
or
dual-use solar
, maximises land-use efficiency, provides shade for crops and creates additional benefits for farmers.
Design and Functioning of Agrivoltaic Systems
An agrivoltaic system integratesagricultural infrastructure with solar installations, adapted to local farming conditions. The technology operates through various key elements:
Elevated Solar Structures:
Instead of placing solar panels directly on the ground, they are mounted on structures high enough to let sunlight and rain reach the crops below. These elevated solar panels for agriculture also allow farmers to move their equipment underneath without any trouble.
Partial shading:
The panels provide shade, which helps protect crops from extreme heat and reduces water evaporation from the soil. This creates a cooler, more stable environment for plants to grow, especially in hot or dry regions.
Dual Land Productivity:
Agrivoltaics optimises land use by integrating crop cultivation or livestock rearing with solar power generation, supplying electricity for farm activities and creating an additional revenue stream through surplus power sales to the grid.
Agrivoltaics Development in India
As of August 2025, India had
36 operational agrivoltaics projects
with an
installed capacity of 37.54 megawatts, alongside 10 pilot projects under development
. These Projects span diverse agroclimatic regions and include elevated structures, interspace layouts and tracking systems, reflecting India’s evolving approach to integrating solar power generation with agricultural production.
India’s Agrivoltaic Potential
India holds significant potential for agrivoltaics.
Estimates place the country’s agrivoltaic potential between
3,000 GW and nearly 14,000 GW
, highlighting the scale of opportunity at the intersection of agriculture and renewable energy. Agrivoltaic systems can also create profits diversificationfor farmers. In some cases, annual earnings could rise from around
Rs.
60,000 per acre to over
Rs.
1 lakh per acre
.
Scope for Agrivoltaics Developments
Land Suitability:
The GIS-based national screening identified
47.35 million hectares
of “restricted cropland” suitable for AgriPV after applying environmental, agronomic, and technical filters, reflecting a conservative, climate-resilient land base.
Crop Compatibility:
Fruits, vegetables, spices and medicinal plants offer promising options for cultivation alongside solar installations.
High-potential states
include Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh, which collectively account for nearly 50 per cent of India’s estimated AgriPV power generation potential, driven
by favourable combinationof cropland availability, solar resource, and agro-climatic conditions.
Moderate potential
is observed in Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Telangana, Bihar, and West Bengal.
The southern, western, and central regions exhibit the most favourable combination of solar irradiance, land availability, and horticultural intensity for large-scale deployment.
Government Initiatives in Agrivoltaics Development
The Government of India has undertaken a range of policy, research, technology development, and implementation measures to advance agrivoltaics adoption and expansion across the country.
Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (PM KUSUM):
Launched in February 2019, the scheme encourages solar energy adoption in agriculture, reduces dependence on diesel and creates opportunities for farmers to diversify their earnings. It envisages central financial assistance of approximately
Rs.
34,422 crore. It also enables decentralised solar power generation and solarisation of agricultural pumps, creating avenues of development for solar energy integration with farming.
PM KUSUM Scheme
Centre of Excellence on Agrivoltaics:
The National Institute of Solar Energy, in collaboration with the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s Indian Agricultural Research Institute, has established a CoE for agrivoltaics research, demonstration and capacity building. It has undertaken pilot projects, including a 100-kilowatt agrivoltaic system at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute.
India Agrivoltaics Alliance
The
India Agrivoltaics Alliance (IAA
), anchored by the National Solar Energy Federation of India (NSEFI), is a multi-stakeholder platform advancing the dual use of land for solar energy generation and agriculture. Launched in 2023, the Alliance has grown to over 40 members and works with government ministries and industry stakeholders to advance agrivoltaics through policy advocacy, research and on-the-ground implementation. It develops knowledge resources, promotes pilot projects and supports scalable business models to improve land productivity, diversify farmer incomes and strengthen rural energy access.
State-specific Initiatives
Several states are facilitating solar energy in agriculture through region-specific schemes.
Mukhyamantri Saur Krushi Vahini Yojana 2.0, Maharashtra:
The scheme drives solar power generation through 16,000 megawatts of solar projects across approximately 35,000 acres of government and private land to support electricity supply to agricultural consumers.
Kisan Suryoday Yojana, Gujarat:
Expands solar energy utilisation to meet farmers’ electricity needs by providing daytime power supply for agricultural activities, with a planned supply window of up to 16 hours daily, from 5:00 AM to 9:00 PM, through the phased commissioning of solar and other non-conventional energy generation plants.
Surya Raitha Scheme, Karnataka
:
The scheme advances solar-powered irrigation pumps and allows farmers to earn from surplus electricity. Solar pumps can help farmers access energy for watering their crops while reducing dependence on diesel-powered pumps.
The Government of India, alongside state governments, is advancing the use of solar energy in agriculture through policy measures and targeted programmes. These efforts are shaping India’s agrivoltaics landscape by creating opportunities for the co-location of solar power generation and agricultural production.
Powering Prosperity Through the Convergence of Farms and Clean Energy
Agrivoltaics offers India an opportunity to strengthen agricultural livelihoods while advancing environmental sustainability. By combining food production with renewable energy generation, it can offer scope for more efficient land use, conserve water under suitable conditions and create greater financial resilience. The Government of India’s initiatives, including PM-KUSUM and proposed measures to expand agrivoltaics, reflect efforts to connect rural development with clean energy goals. As implementation grows, locally suitable designs, scientific research and farmer participation will be essential to balance agricultural productivity with energy needs. This approach can contribute to a more resilient and sustainable future for India.Greater financial resilience

title: Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan - Rabi 2026
subtitle: “Soil Health and Sustainable Agriculture”

content:
Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan (KBA)-Rabi 2026 is a nationwide campaign running from 22 October to 30 November 2026. It promotes soil health, balanced fertiliser use, and sustainable agriculture across 34 States and Union Territories, over 700 districts and 50,000 villages, targeting
around 50 lakh farmers.
Key priorities include balanced nutrient management, natural farming, crop residue management, crop diversification and climate-resilient agriculture. The campaign envisages 4,150 teams involving KVKs and ATMA, supported by over 12,000 scientists and ATMA functionaries. The initiative seeks to conduct 50,000 field demonstrations and 11,750 structured training sessions. The campaign projects a social media outreach of 1.5 crore farmers, with an envisaged expansion of overall digital outreach to 2.5 crore.
The Foundation of Farming Lies Beneath
Soil health is fundamental to agricultural productivity, food security, and rural livelihoods. With more than
46 percent
of India’s workforce engaged in agriculture and allied activities, soil health influences food systems and economic stability. Healthy soils support higher crop yields and reduce dependence on external inputs.
Recognising the importance of soil health,
Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan (KBA) - Rabi 2026
“Swasth Dhara, Samriddh Kisan”
is envisaged as a nationwide campaign from
22 October to 30 November 2026.
It follows a convergence-based approach, bringing together agricultural departments, research institutions, and field-level functionaries to promote balanced, judicious fertiliser use and sustainable nutrient management. The campaign aims to promote sustainable agriculture, improve soil health, and encourage the judicious use of agricultural resources. It also promotes natural farming, water conservation, and efficient use of natural resources. It addresses concerns such as imbalanced nutrient application, declining soil organic matter, rising cultivation costs, and the degradation of natural resources.
The initiatives also emphasise capacity building, farm mechanisation, and demonstrations of improved agricultural technologies, including regenerative agriculture practices (
farming methods focused on restoring soil health and enhancing biodiversity).
The campaign covers
34
States and Union Territories, over
700
districts and
50,000
villages. It aims to reach around
50 lakh
farmers through coordinated activities. States and Union Territories have been instructed to prioritise
100 high fertiliser-consuming districts
to strengthen outreach and promote balanced nutrient management.
Through its wide reach and field-level activities, the campaign seeks to bring farmers, scientists and agricultural institutions together. This coordinated effort is expected to encourage informed farming decisions and greater adoption of sustainable agricultural practices.
Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan
(From 1 to 30 June 2026)
Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan was launched nationwide on 1 June 2026 as a month-long campaign to promote soil health, balanced fertiliser use and sustainable agricultural practices. The campaign deployed
1,657
multidisciplinary teams for direct field-level engagement. The initiative achieved significant outreach, conducting over 1.34 lakh awareness events for 92.44 lakh farmers, and 6,685 training sessions on green manuring and bio-fertilisers, benefiting 4.94 lakh farmers. Additionally, 3,167 field demonstrations and 4,779 interactive programs provided hands-on learning. A further
4,916
Janpratinidhi Sammelans, including those involving fertiliser and input dealers, strengthened grassroots engagement.. Overall, the campaign directly reached around
1.07
crore
farmers and other stakeholders, while social media outreach covered approximately
4.5 crore
citizens.
Key Objectives of Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan - Rabi 2026
The campaign aims to encourage farmers to adopt location-specific, science-based practices that improve input-use efficiency and support climate-resilient agriculture.
Balanced Nutrient Management:
Promote General Fertiliser Recommendations (GFR) based nutrient management and the 4R Principle of fertiliser use -  Right source, Right rate, Right time, and Right place. This method ensures balanced, efficient fertiliser use aligned with Rabi crop requirements.
Natural Farming:
Encourage the adoption of natural farming through awareness campaigns, capacity building, demonstrations and farmer-to-farmer learning.
Integrated Nutrient Management (INM):
Promote INM and the use of suitable organic and biological inputs through awareness, capacity building and demonstrations.

Dhaincha and Green Gram Offer a Path to Healthier Soils
In the rice-growing areas of East Champaran, Bihar, maintaining soil fertility while managing fertiliser use is an important concern for farmers. Declining soil organic carbon and micronutrient deficiencies add to the challenge. Under Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan-2026, the ICAR-Mahatma Gandhi Integrated Farming Research Institute (MGIFRI), Motihari, Bihar, highlighted how green manuring and biological nitrogen fixation can support soil health.
At the farmer outreach programme at the Pantoka Panchayat in Raxaul Block, East Champaran District, Bihar, farmers were encouraged to combine farmyard manure, compost, biofertilisers and crop residues with recommended fertiliser doses. The discussions covered rice nursery management and alternatives to crop residue burning, including composting, mulching and vermicomposting.
Scientists also emphasised the use of
dhaincha
(
Sesbania
sp.) and summer green gram in rice-based cropping systems.
Dhaincha
can contribute around 50-60 kg of nitrogen per hectare, equivalent to 110-130 kg of urea. Summer green gram can contribute 25-30 kg of nitrogen per hectare, equivalent to 55-65 kg of urea. These crops can help reduce fertiliser requirements while improving soil organic matter and biological activity.
The programme brought together 62 farmers, including 41 women. Participants expressed willingness to adopt green manuring and balanced nutrient management.
Bringing the Campaign to Farmers: Institutional Roles and Responsibilities
State/UT Department of Agriculture:
Responsible for campaign planning and implementation, issuing necessary instructions, convening preparatory meetings, approving district-level schedules, mobilising field personnel and convergence partners, facilitating access to schemes and services, and consolidating reports.
Agricultural Technology Management Agencies (ATMA) and District Agriculture Administration:
Responsible for coordinating campaign activities across district, block and village levels, preparing micro-plans, mobilising farmers and community institutions, facilitating venues, field access, IEC materials and logistics, and maintaining attendance and activity records.
ICAR Institutes, Agricultural Technology Application Research Institutes (ATARIs), Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs), and Agricultural Universities (Knowledge Partners):
Provide science-based technical guidance and location-specific recommendations, nominate resource persons, support training, conduct demonstrations and farmer-scientist interactions when requested, prepare or validate technical IEC materials and advisories, share research evidence, and document lessons. Their role does not extend to State-level implementation, administrative control, enforcement or expenditure responsibilities unless separately authorised.

4,150 teams
involving KVKs and ATMA. More than
12,000 scientists
and ATMA functionaries are expected to help implement it. Through ATMA and ICAR, the campaign aims to reach approximately
one crore participants
.
Other State Departments and Agencies:
Support and facilitate campaign activities, as relevant to their respective mandates, through coordinated engagement by departments and agencies responsible for horticulture, soil and water conservation, irrigation, animal husbandry, rural development, cooperatives, Panchayati Raj, environment, agricultural marketing and allied sectors.
Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs), Self-Help Groups (SHGs), Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), Custom Hiring Centres (CHCs) and Progressive Farmers:
Support local mobilisation, peer learning, demonstration visits and dissemination of validated advisories among farmers.
Media and Communication Partners:
Facilitate the dissemination of approved campaign messages through local media, community radio, WhatsApp, Kisan Sarathi and other appropriate communication platforms, while ensuring the accuracy and verification of agronomic information shared with farmers.
Driving Farmer Awareness and Outreach
The campaign combines farmer awareness, capacity building, field demonstrations, practical exposure visits, and digital outreach to promote improved agricultural practices, strengthen technical knowledge, and extend the reach of campaign messages among farmers.
Awareness Creation for Various Activities
The campaign seeks to enhance farmers’ awareness and understanding of General Fertiliser Recommendations GFR-based nutrient management, natural farming, Integrated Nutrient Management (INM), Crop Residue Management (CRM), and improved technologies for oilseed and pulse production. It also disseminates information on Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for implementing contingency plans in drought-affected districts and key government schemes related to agriculture.
Each of the
950 ICAR institute teams
is assigned three village visits per week, while the 700 KVK teams are expected to undertake four visits per week. Each visit targets the participation of 100 farmers.
Over a five-week period, the campaign envisages
5,650 awareness programmes
, with an estimated outreach
of 28.25 lakh farmers.
Capacity Building of Farmers
Training programmes are designed to strengthen
farmers’ knowledge and technical capacities
in Integrated Nutrient Management (INM), Crop Residue Management (CRM), natural farming, improved oilseed and pulse production practices, Integrated Pest Management (IPM), and other relevant thematic areas.
Each of the 950 ICAR institute teams is expected to conduct
one training programme
per week
, while the 700 KVK teams are assigned
two programmes per week
. Each programme targets 40 participants.
Over a five-week period, the campaign envisages 11,750 training programmes, with an estimated outreach of
4.70 lakh farmers.
Demonstrations at Farmers’ Fields
ICAR institutes and Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) organise
field demonstrations at selected farmers’
fields
to illustrate the potential and
benefits of improved agricultural technologies
. These demonstrations enable farmers to assess scientific interventions and compare their outcomes with existing farming practices. The key areas covered include Green Ammonia, Crop Residue Management (CRM), Integrated Nutrient Management (INM), Integrated Pest Management (IPM), natural farming, Integrated Crop Management (ICM) for oilseeds and pulses, biofertilisers, and organic and biological inputs.
The campaign envisages
50,000 field demonstrations
, comprising 40,000 by KVKs and 10,000 by ICAR institutes.
With an intended participation of 20 farmers per demonstration, the initiative targets an estimated outreach of
10 lakh farmers.
Field Days, Harvest Days and Exposure Visits
Field days, harvest events and exposure visits to demonstration sites constitute an integral component of the campaign’s
“Seeing is Believing” approach
. These activities provide farmers with first-hand opportunities to observe improved agricultural technologies, understand their practical applications and assess their benefits under field conditions.
Each of the
1,650 teams
is assigned to organise three field or harvest days and two exposure visits during the crop season, with each activity targeting approximately 125 farmers.
These activities are expected to collectively reach approximately
10 lakh farmers
.
Social Media Outreach
Digital platforms serve as an important channel for disseminating information on improved agricultural practices, technical advisories, and campaign-related activities, thereby extending the campaign’s outreach beyond field-level interventions.
Organising teams to disseminate daily updates through
WhatsApp, Facebook, X, and other appropriate digital platforms.
The campaign projects a social media outreach of
1.5 crore farmers
, with an envisaged expansion of overall digital outreach to

Connecting Farmers with Schemes and Services
The campaign undertakes targeted awareness initiatives to familiarise farmers with key agricultural schemes, services and practices. These include
PM-KISAN, balanced pesticide use, Soil Health Cards, the applicable fertiliser sale framework and the potential benefits of trade agreements.
It also facilitates the creation and updating of Farmers’ IDs and disseminates information on crop insurance coverage under the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY). In addition, saturation drives under the Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme seek to facilitate eligible
farmers’
access to institutional credit.
Collectively, these interventions seek to strengthen farmers’ awareness of government support mechanisms and improve their access to essential agricultural services, formal credit and risk-mitigation instruments, thereby reinforcing the institutional and financial foundations of farm livelihoods.
Strengthening the Foundations of Sustainable Agriculture
The Khet Bachaao Abhiyaan-Rabi 2026
seeks to place soil health and sustainable resource management at the centre of agricultural development. Through convergence among scientific institutions, government departments, extension networks and farming communities, it aims to translate scientific knowledge into location-specific agricultural practices. Its integrated approach combines
farmer awareness, capacity building, field demonstrations and digital outreach
to promote improved farming practices. Alongside balanced nutrient management, natural farming and efficient input use, the campaign emphasises crop diversification, residue management, integrated pest management and climate resilience. Its focus on institutional coordination and farmer participation also strengthens grassroots extension mechanisms and access to agricultural services.
These interventions support resource-efficient farming systems, healthier soils and resilient agricultural livelihoods, contributing to the broader vision of
Viksit Bharat.
Furthermore, the campaign supports progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Zero Hunger (SDG 2) and Climate Action (SDG 13).
